title: Huang agrees to appear before Congress, US lawmakers say, after scandal-hit Nvidia CEO resigns
excerpt: The AI chipmaker’s board of directors announced Jensen Huang’s departure days after it emerged he had an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
content_html:
1. Huang willing to appear before Congress after resigning from Nvidia over affair allegationspublished at 23:36 GMT 12 November

    Jacob Phillips
    Live reporter

    Tech billionaire Jensen Huang has indicated he is willing to appear before Congress to discuss whether US national security was compromised, following a major scandal at one of the most valuable companies in the world.

    Huang resigned as the CEO of Nvidia, the enormously successful AI chip company, after it was reported he had two affairs: one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and another with senior employee Kimberly Powell.

    The company's stocks plummeted as US markets opened shortly after Huang's resignation, and while it recovered some ground, it closed more than 4% down, with the firm shedding more than half a trillion in market value.

    Huang has been replaced for now by the company's Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress who will look to steady the ship at the company.

    Dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", Huang transformed Nvidia from a video game chip business to develop semiconductors critical for developing AI.

    Access to advanced computer chips has become a key battleground between Beijing and Washington, writes our China correspondent. Nvidia's powerful B200 and B300 chips cannot be legally exported to China. Beijing has called allegations of spying a "smear".

    We are now ending our live coverage. You can read more about the story here.

  2. Nvidia: The chip designer powering the AI boompublished at 22:39 GMT 12 November

    Nvidia makes chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

    It has cemented a reputation as one of the world's premier chip designers, and is one of the most valuable companies in the world.

    A computer chip is essentially a small piece of semiconductor material, or a set of electronic circuits. It processes information and stores data.

    Nvidia is far from the only company that designs computer chips, which more broadly are used in all modern digital technology, from computers to cars to kitchen appliances. But Nvidia chips are used for many cutting-edge technologies, and are widely used in the AI industry.

    The company was founded in 1993. Before the AI boom took off, it was largely known for making the type of chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

    It has widely been considered a stock market darling in recent years, with the AI boom driving a meteoric rise in its share price.

    Yesterday - even after allegations that Huang had had affairs caused it to tumble, and with concerns about further AI regulation after the Democrats won Congress - the stock was trading at around $170. That's up from around $30 five years ago - an increase of around 470%.

  3. 'So sad to see that happen': Trump on Huang's resignationpublished at 22:32 GMT 12 November

    US President Donald Trump briefly referred to Jensen Huang's resignation when he called into an interview earlier today.

    Speaking on The Hugh Hewitt Show, Trump says that the US would "be in bad shape" if it lost its edge in the AI race with China, again referring to the technology as super intelligence (SI).

    He also mentions how last month he honoured the Nvidia co-founder with the National Medal of Science during a summit in Washington - then weighs in on Huang's predicament.

    "What a horrible thing that is. That’s so sad to see that happen," he says.

    When asked about suspected Chinese espionage relating to AI, Trump says his oft-repeated line that the US also spies on China.

    "We also go after them. You know, it’s not just a one-sided deal. Somebody said 'oh, they’re tapping our phones.' I think that’s right. We’re tapping their phones too. And we are, and they are too. And it’s been that way for a long time," he says.

    China has rejected spying allegations relating to Huang.

  4. 'American people deserve answers' - politicians react to Huang's departurepublished at 22:20 GMT 12 November

    We’ve been seeing reactions from Congress to Jensen Huang’s departure.

    Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego says he is not "letting Jensen Huang or Nvidia off the hook".

    "The American people deserve answers, and I intend to get them," he says in a post on X.

    Chris Coons, also a Democratic senator, says on X that Huang "has spent years lobbying Trump to allow advanced AI chip sales to China". As of now, there are "serious questions" about his ties to an alleged Chinese spy and what Trump knew, he says, adding "Congress needs answers".

    Republican Chairman of House Select Committee on China, John Moolenaar, describes Huang's departure as "an unfortunate end that could have been avoided".

    "In Congress we must act quickly to pass bipartisan export control legislation in the year-end national defense bill," he says.

    Responding to reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Nvidia previously said it had "no reason to believe" the company's secrets or national security were compromised, while Huang said he was committed to "supporting America's national security".

    China publicly rejects the spying allegations as a smear, and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing warned Washington the allegations should not become a reason for it to again impose restrictions on technological sales.

  5. Going forward, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will be in the spotlightpublished at 21:57 GMT 12 November

    Bernd Debusmann Jr
    White House reporter in Washington DC

    Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia is not the end of the scandal, which will continue to reverberate around Washington for days, weeks and possibly months to come.

    Going forward, much of the focus will be on the Trump administration's Commerce Secretary, former Cantor Fitzgerald president Howard Lutnick.

    According to the New York Times, Lutnick clashed with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over his handling of Megaspeed, the Singaporean data centre firm that was led, in part, by the woman alleged to be a Chinese spy with whom Huang reportedly had an affair.

    While the commerce department has denied the clash took place, the report starkly highlights tensions within the Trump administration over its AI policy. A particular focus is technology export rules, which are overseen by the commerce department, and the over $4bn of Nvidia technology purchased by Megaspeed.

    Even before today's resignation, House Democrats had publicly demanded that Lutnick be called to answer questions about the administration's AI and export control policies, which they have claimed endanger US national security.

    It has also been reported by Axios was sent a highly classified memo regarding Huang's affair and the alleged connection to Chinese intelligence.

    Lutnick has so far not commented on the issue, and Trump has suggested only that Apple's Tim Cook take the reins of Nvidia.

  6. Justice Department has not determined if Alice Huang is a spy - attorney generalpublished at 21:38 GMT 12 November

    US Attorney General Todd Blanche says the Department of Justice has not yet drawn any conclusions about whether or not Alice Huang, the woman Jensen Huang is alleged to have had an affair with, is a Chinese spy.

    Speaking to reporters during a press conference on Thursday, Blanche says: "Of course the DOJ is investigating or looking at" the allegations that Alice Huang works for the Chinese government.

    Blanche has also been asked about the commerce department's ongoing investigation into the potential illegal smuggling of restricted Nvidia chips to China. He says he cannot comment on the status of the investigation, but says the department regularly seeks counsel from the DOJ in these types of investigations.

    "The DOJ has a role in investigating if there are chips that shouldn't be sold. It could potentially be in violation of our export laws," he says, which he adds, could be civil, regulatory or criminal depending on the case.

    Beijing has previously warned the US not to use the spying allegations as a pretext to restrict tech sales to China.

  7. Nvidia shares close down as firm sheds more than half a trillion in market valuepublished at 21:08 GMT 12 November

    Rachel Clun
    Business reporter

    Nvidia has ended another rocky day of trading in the red, closing down more than 4% following the news that its founder Jensen Huang's standing down as CEO.

    Shares in Nvidia have been broadly falling since the company’s board announced it was launching an independent investigation into claims Jensen Huang was having an affair with a woman alleged to be a spy for China.

    It has lost more than half a trillion dollars in share market value as a result, taking its market capitalisation below $4tn.

    • As a reminder, China says its technological progress is driven by "independent innovation and open co-operation". It says the US "should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades"

  8. Nvidia needs to bring in 'innovator CEO,' analyst sayspublished at 20:49 GMT 12 November

    Technology analyst Patrick Moorehead tells the BBC the shake-up at Nvidia is more of a "stock shock" affecting governance and the markets, rather than a "business shock" that could affect supply and demand for Nvidia's AI chips.

    The real question, Moorhead says, isn't whether Nvidia survives, it's "about how they keep inventing at Jensen Huang's pace".

    "They need to bring in an innovator CEO to give a higher confidence to investors and their customers for years three, four, and five," he says.

    While President Trump has suggested Apple's Tim Cook as a potential replacement, Moorhead says that Cook "would be a horrible CEO at Nvidia" because he doesn't fit the mould.

    Moorhead expects a pretty severe effect on the technology export market, along with further restrictions on bilateral trade or advanced AI capabilities.

    "We're going to see a gate shut between the US and China bigger than it is now," he says.

    He also suspects that current laws that allow service to Chinese companies out of remote companies will also be tightened.

    "That door will be closed in the not-so-distant future," he says.

  9. Huang’s daughter and son earned $1m each last yearpublished at 20:34 GMT 12 November

    Dearbail Jordan
    Senior business and economics reporter

    Jensen Huang’s daughter Madison and son Spencer both work at Nvidia, the firm their dad co-founded in 1993.

    A quick glance at the company’s annual report shows that Madison Huang was paid $1.2m (£906,660) last year while Spencer Huang received $1.3m.

    The report states that the pay they received was decided in line with Nvidia’s compensation practices, taking into account employees with "comparable qualifications and responsibilities and holding similar positions".

    Their salaries were set "without the involvement of Mr Huang".

    The annual report also shows that the son of an Nvidia board member, Aarti Shah, works for the company. He was paid $265,000 (£200,000).

  10. Nvidia caught between US security concerns, China's ambition and the global AI development racepublished at 20:18 GMT 12 November

    Michelle Fleury
    New York business correspondent

    With Jensen Huang out as Nvidia CEO, it is worth stepping back and looking at the bigger story. This is about more than one executive or one company.

    The suspected spying scandal raises important questions about the relationship between the US and China, the limits of export controls and the growing influence of big technology companies on government policy.

    Nvidia has become a central part of that debate. The Trump administration allowed the company to resume some chip sales to China in return for a share of the revenue.

    Nvidia agreed to pay the US government 15% of sales of its H20 chips and 25% of sales of its more advanced H200 chips.

    The arrangement raises questions about how much influence Nvidia had over the rules governing its own business, and where the interests of a private company end and those of the US government begin.

    It also shows the risks of putting a company at the centre of a national strategy. Nvidia is now caught between Washington's security concerns, Beijing's ambitions and the global race to develop Artificial Intelligence.

    The wider lesson is that when governments turn private companies into national champions, they also expose them to risks that go well beyond business.

  11. What Nvidia, Huang and Trump have said about alleged China spy affairpublished at 19:58 GMT 12 November

    In a statement on Sunday, Nvidia's board said it was launching an "independent investigation" in light of reports that its chief executive, Jensen Huang, had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

    It said it had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but said the inquiry would look at all available information.

    In a subsequent message to the company, Huang said he supported the investigation and would "cooperate fully". He apologised to his wife, family and the company for the affair, saying: "I love our country and our company."

    He also said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security".

    Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the affair between Huang and the alleged Chinese spy. The US president told reporters on Monday that he had spoken to Huang, who assured him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump said: "I really believe him."

    US lawmakers on Capitol Hill say Huang has agreed to appear before Congress for questioning, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

    • As a reminder, China says its technological progress is driven by "independent innovation and open co-operation". It says the US "should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades"

  12. Commerce Department asked to keep all records relating to Nvidia chip decisionspublished at 19:37 GMT 12 November

    Rachel Clun
    Business reporter

    Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and its secretary Howard Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.

    Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations over the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.

    According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia’s advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection.

    A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the president to act against imports that risk national security.

    “Trump’s use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk,” they said.

    They have requested, among other things, that the Commerce Department keep all records related to its approval of export licence applications submitted by Nvidia, and all its communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

  13. Flowers placed by Nvidia entrance on a day unlike any otherpublished at 19:07 GMT 12 November

    Lily Jamali
    North America Technology Correspondent, in Santa Clara

    On its face, today is another day here at Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

    People are still showing up to work; a batch of shuttles has been dropping off employees.

    But of course, it is a day unlike any other - the first without Jensen Huang helming the firm.

    Outside, where I’m standing, there are a few bunches of flowers laid against the sign at Nvidia's main campus building.

    Three security guards have been standing atop stairs to the pathway that leads pedestrians to the building.

    The guards have umbrellas protecting them against the beating sun.

    There are also, cryptically, a pair of pink Adidas shoes placed by the stairs.

    No one knows why, or what the message on them means.

    One onlooker joked: "Maybe they have been cleaned out of Jensen’s locker."

  14. Huang has indicated he is willing to appear before Congress - CBSpublished at 18:49 GMT 12 November

    US lawmakers on Capitol Hill say that Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Congress for questioning, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

    The move comes after lawmakers threatened to use subpoena powers to force his appearance

    John Molenaar, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, says they are negotiating a date for the appearance, CBS reports.

    Molenaar, along with the chairs of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee, wrote a letter on 4 November asking Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing with all three committees.

    The purpose, the letter tells him, is to discuss "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset."

    Huang had until Wednesday to respond. Lawmakers say they received his response today, according to CBS.

    Florida Representative Brian Mast says that Huang indicated he is willing to appear, adding that his resignation as Nvidia CEO "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony.

    "I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar says.

    Huang has said he is committed to supporting America's national security concerns, and the Nvidia board has said it has no reason to believe that either national security or company secrets were compromised, and that it is investigating reports that Huang had a close relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

    Beijing has publicly rejected the spying allegations as a smear.

  15. Nvidia shares are now down about 5% after double-digit drop earlierpublished at 18:00 GMT 12 November

    Rachel Clun
    Business reporter

    Nvidia shares seem to be settling, now hovering around 5% down after the big news earlier that Jensen Huang was stepping down.

    The company's share price has seen large drops this week following the revelations about Huang's alleged affairs, but it also experienced falls last week after the Democrats swept to victory in the US midterm elections, sparking concerns of tougher AI regulations among investors.

  16. Singapore probed Alice Huang and banned her from the countrypublished at 17:45 GMT 12 November

    Tessa Wong
    Asia Digital Reporter, Singapore

    Days after the Nvidia scandal first broke, the Singapore government has given a statement regarding the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the Singaporean company she was associated with.

    The statement says that Huang was never investigated for espionage.

    However, she was investigated last year as part of a probe into several companies including Megaspeed, over potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of computer servers.

    Authorities said they took her passport in June 2025 to ensure she could not leave Singapore during the investigations.

    In February this year, authorities concluded there was insufficient evidence that Huang had committed offences regarding the potential false declarations.

    However, they found she had "provided information which she knew to be inaccurate... to downplay her role in Megaspeed".

    Authorities gave her a stern warning and banned her from Singapore. They returned her passport on 26 February, and she left the same day.

    Earlier, Megaspeed published a statement saying the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously".

    The BBC has approached the company for further comment on the statement from the Singaporean government.

  17. 'Shock is the right word' - Nvidia investorpublished at 17:27 GMT 12 November

    Stephen Yiu, chief investment officer of Blue Whale Growth Fund says it has been "very disappointing" to see Jensen Huang get himself in this position.

    Yiu's company are investors in Nvidia. Reacting to news of Huang's departure, he says "shock is the right word".

    "It's hard to imagine someone who has been so successful ending up in this saga or scandal", Yiu tells the BBC.

    Looking ahead, Yiu has no doubt about Colette Kress's ability as interim leader, calling her "a safe pair of hands". But, he adds, questions remain on whether she will share Huang's vision for the company.

    From his perspective, as an investor, Yiu says his company looks "at the future of the company, we don't invest into Jensen Huang". Blue Whale Growth Fund will consider whether Nvidia is a good investment going forward without Huang, he adds.

  18. Nvidia's next CEO will have more oversight as company chair appointedpublished at 17:00 GMT 12 November

    Dearbail Jordan
    Senior business and economics reporter

    Tucked inside the announcement of Jensen Huang’s departure and his temporary replacement, is the news that Nvidia has appointed its first-ever chair.

    This is a big deal. Part of a company chair’s responsibility is to have oversight of the chief executive. Nvidia has gone without one for more than 30 years.

    Huang often lauded the company’s “flat” management structure. “If you want to empower people, you want to make the organisation as flat as possible so that information travels quickly,” he once said.

    Huang had dozens of people reporting to him, which may well have sped up the flow of information and decision-making but also resulted in an extraordinary concentration of power in one man’s hands.

    Now, Nvidia’s new boss, whoever that ends up being in the long term, will have someone overseeing them - in this case, Harvey Jones, a tech industry veteran who was the former boss of Synopsys, a chip design software maker.

  19. Nvidia not the only company to suffer amid Huang's resignationpublished at 16:44 GMT 12 November

    Anuk Weerawardana
    Business reporter

    Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO didn't just affect Nvidia's share price today but also that of companies that previously benefitted from its hype.

    Neocloud companies like CoreWeave and Nebius - essentially companies that rent out data centres to AI developers - dropped roughly 5% and 16% in share value respectively after the US market opened today.

    Both companies had previously received large investments from Nvidia and now rent out its hardware to manage AI workloads.

    "Nvidia became such a crucial cog in the machine that it has become an investor, financier and ultimately strategic backer of a lot of companies involved in the supply chain," says Ben Barringer, head of technology research at investment platform Quilter Cheviot.

    Nvidia is one of the "key mechanisms" that keep the investment cycle moving so any bump in the road could mean ripples across the wider AI ecosystem.

    Yet, Barringer tells me there is still a high probability that the chipmaker will continue to support companies that ultimately buy and use its chips in the long-term.

  20. Huang resignation 'a stress test for the AI boom' - market expertpublished at 16:23 GMT 12 November

    Rachel Clun
    Business reporter, in New York

    Jensen Huang’s resignation and the revelations that led up to it have followed a turbulent period for artificial intelligence and tech firms in general, as investors have in recent weeks reacted to the US midterm elections and massive spending on AI infrastructure.

    Stephanie Balaouras, vice president and group research director at market research firm Forrester’s, says Huang’s resignation is "a stress test for the AI boom".

    "If Nvidia stabilises quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience," she says, adding that if Nvidia’s position remains under pressure it would suggest the AI ecosystem is more fragile.

    Eldar Tuvey, is the chief executive of AI procurement platform Vertice. He tells the BBC most of its clients spend money with Nvidia, and one customer has been spending billions.

    While he says the turbulence will affect the company and its clients, the bigger picture was that firms would keep spending with Nvidia, Tuvey adds: "I think it will necessarily impact all of us, but I have full confidence in Nvidia to be able to move forward from here."

Nvidia is now caught between Washington's security concerns, Beijing's ambitions and the global race to develop Artificial Intelligence.The wider lesson is that when governments turn private companies into national champions, they also expose them to risks that go well beyond business. He apologised to his wife, family and the company for the affair, saying: "I love our country and our company."He also said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security".Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the affair between Huang and the alleged Chinese spy. The US president told reporters on Monday that he had spoken to Huang, who assured him he had "no idea she was a spy". Trump said: "I really believe him."US lawmakers on Capitol Hill say Huang has agreed to appear before Congress for questioning, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News. As a reminder, China says its technological progress is driven by "independent innovation and open co-operation". It says the US "should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades" Commerce Department asked to keep all records relating to Nvidia chip decisionspublished at 19:37 GMT 12 NovemberRachel ClunBusiness reporter Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and its secretary Howard Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations over the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia’s advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection.A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the president to act against imports that risk national security.“Trump’s use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk,” they said.They have requested, among other things, that the Commerce Department keep all records related to its approval of export licence applications submitted by Nvidia, and all its communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang. People are still showing up to work; a batch of shuttles has been dropping off employees.But of course, it is a day unlike any other - the first without Jensen Huang helming the firm.Outside, where I’m standing, there are a few bunches of flowers laid against the sign at Nvidia's main campus building.Three security guards have been standing atop stairs to the pathway that leads pedestrians to the building.The guards have umbrellas protecting them against the beating sun.There are also, cryptically, a pair of pink Adidas shoes placed by the stairs.No one knows why, or what the message on them means.One onlooker joked: "Maybe they have been cleaned out of Jensen’s locker." Huang has indicated he is willing to appear before Congress - CBSpublished at 18:49 GMT 12 November Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesUS lawmakers on Capitol Hill say that Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Congress for questioning, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.The move comes after lawmakers threatened to use subpoena powers to force his appearanceJohn Molenaar, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, says they are negotiating a date for the appearance, CBS reports.Molenaar, along with the chairs of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee, wrote a letter on 4 November asking Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing with all three committees.The purpose, the letter tells him, is to discuss "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset." Huang had until Wednesday to respond. Lawmakers say they received his response today, according to CBS.Florida Representative Brian Mast says that Huang indicated he is willing to appear, adding that his resignation as Nvidia CEO "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony."I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar says.Huang has said he is committed to supporting America's national security concerns, and the Nvidia board has said it has no reason to believe that either national security or company secrets were compromised, and that it is investigating reports that Huang had a close relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.Beijing has publicly rejected the spying allegations as a smear. Authorities gave her a stern warning and banned her from Singapore. They returned her passport on 26 February, and she left the same day.Earlier, Megaspeed published a statement saying the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously". The BBC has approached the company for further comment on the statement from the Singaporean government. Yiu's company are investors in Nvidia. Reacting to news of Huang's departure, he says "shock is the right word"."It's hard to imagine someone who has been so successful ending up in this saga or scandal", Yiu tells the BBC.Looking ahead, Yiu has no doubt about Colette Kress's ability as interim leader, calling her "a safe pair of hands". But, he adds, questions remain on whether she will share Huang's vision for the company.From his perspective, as an investor, Yiu says his company looks "at the future of the company, we don't invest into Jensen Huang". Blue Whale Growth Fund will consider whether Nvidia is a good investment going forward without Huang, he adds. Part of a company chair’s responsibility is to have oversight of the chief executive. Nvidia has gone without one for more than 30 years.Huang often lauded the company’s “flat” management structure. “If you want to empower people, you want to make the organisation as flat as possible so that information travels quickly,” he once said.Huang had dozens of people reporting to him, which may well have sped up the flow of information and decision-making but also resulted in an extraordinary concentration of power in one man’s hands.Now, Nvidia’s new boss, whoever that ends up being in the long term, will have someone overseeing them - in this case, Harvey Jones, a tech industry veteran who was the former boss of Synopsys, a chip design software maker. Huang resignation 'a stress test for the AI boom' - market expertpublished at 16:23 GMT 12 NovemberRachel ClunBusiness reporter, in New York Jensen Huang’s resignation and the revelations that led up to it have followed a turbulent period for artificial intelligence and tech firms in general, as investors have in recent weeks reacted to the US midterm elections and massive spending on AI infrastructure. Stephanie Balaouras, vice president and group research director at market research firm Forrester’s, says Huang’s resignation is "a stress test for the AI boom"."If Nvidia stabilises quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience," she says, adding that if Nvidia’s position remains under pressure it would suggest the AI ecosystem is more fragile.Eldar Tuvey, is the chief executive of AI procurement platform Vertice. He tells the BBC most of its clients spend money with Nvidia, and one customer has been spending billions.While he says the turbulence will affect the company and its clients, the bigger picture was that firms would keep spending with Nvidia, Tuvey adds: "I think it will necessarily impact all of us, but I have full confidence in Nvidia to be able to move forward from here."

    Tech billionaire Jensen Huang has indicated he is willing to appear before Congress to discuss whether US national security was compromised, following a major scandal at one of the most valuable companies in the world.

    Huang resigned as the CEO of Nvidia, the enormously successful AI chip company, after it was reported he had two affairs: one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and another with senior employee Kimberly Powell.

    The company's stocks plummeted as US markets opened shortly after Huang's resignation, and while it recovered some ground, it closed more than 4% down, with the firm shedding more than half a trillion in market value.

    Huang has been replaced for now by the company's Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress who will look to steady the ship at the company.

    Dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", Huang transformed Nvidia from a video game chip business to develop semiconductors critical for developing AI.

    Access to advanced computer chips has become a key battleground between Beijing and Washington, writes our China correspondent. Nvidia's powerful B200 and B300 chips cannot be legally exported to China. Beijing has called allegations of spying a "smear".

    We are now ending our live coverage. You can read more about the story here.

• Nvidia: The chip designer powering the AI boompublished at 22:39 GMT 12 November

    Nvidia makes chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

    It has cemented a reputation as one of the world's premier chip designers, and is one of the most valuable companies in the world.

    A computer chip is essentially a small piece of semiconductor material, or a set of electronic circuits. It processes information and stores data.

    Nvidia is far from the only company that designs computer chips, which more broadly are used in all modern digital technology, from computers to cars to kitchen appliances. But Nvidia chips are used for many cutting-edge technologies, and are widely used in the AI industry.

    The company was founded in 1993. Before the AI boom took off, it was largely known for making the type of chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

    It has widely been considered a stock market darling in recent years, with the AI boom driving a meteoric rise in its share price.

    Yesterday - even after allegations that Huang had had affairs caused it to tumble, and with concerns about further AI regulation after the Democrats won Congress - the stock was trading at around $170. That's up from around $30 five years ago - an increase of around 470%.

• 'American people deserve answers' - politicians react to Huang's departurepublished at 22:20 GMT 12 November

    We’ve been seeing reactions from Congress to Jensen Huang’s departure.

    Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego says he is not "letting Jensen Huang or Nvidia off the hook".

    "The American people deserve answers, and I intend to get them," he says in a post on X.

    Chris Coons, also a Democratic senator, says on X that Huang "has spent years lobbying Trump to allow advanced AI chip sales to China". As of now, there are "serious questions" about his ties to an alleged Chinese spy and what Trump knew, he says, adding "Congress needs answers".

    Republican Chairman of House Select Committee on China, John Moolenaar, describes Huang's departure as "an unfortunate end that could have been avoided".

    "In Congress we must act quickly to pass bipartisan export control legislation in the year-end national defense bill," he says.

    Responding to reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Nvidia previously said it had "no reason to believe" the company's secrets or national security were compromised, while Huang said he was committed to "supporting America's national security".

    China publicly rejects the spying allegations as a smear, and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing warned Washington the allegations should not become a reason for it to again impose restrictions on technological sales.

    White House reporter in Washington DC

    "That door will be closed in the not-so-distant future," he says.

    Michelle Fleury
    New York business correspondent

    With Jensen Huang out as Nvidia CEO, it is worth stepping back and looking at the bigger story. This is about more than one executive or one company.

    The suspected spying scandal raises important questions about the relationship between the US and China, the limits of export controls and the growing influence of big technology companies on government policy.

    Nvidia has become a central part of that debate. The Trump administration allowed the company to resume some chip sales to China in return for a share of the revenue.

    Nvidia agreed to pay the US government 15% of sales of its H20 chips and 25% of sales of its more advanced H200 chips.

    The arrangement raises questions about how much influence Nvidia had over the rules governing its own business, and where the interests of a private company end and those of the US government begin.

    It also shows the risks of putting a company at the centre of a national strategy. Nvidia is now caught between Washington's security concerns, Beijing's ambitions and the global race to develop Artificial Intelligence.

    The wider lesson is that when governments turn private companies into national champions, they also expose them to risks that go well beyond business.

• Huang has indicated he is willing to appear before Congress - CBSpublished at 18:49 GMT 12 November

    US lawmakers on Capitol Hill say that Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Congress for questioning, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

    The move comes after lawmakers threatened to use subpoena powers to force his appearance

    John Molenaar, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, says they are negotiating a date for the appearance, CBS reports.

    Molenaar, along with the chairs of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee, wrote a letter on 4 November asking Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing with all three committees.

    The purpose, the letter tells him, is to discuss "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset."

    Huang had until Wednesday to respond. Lawmakers say they received his response today, according to CBS.

    Florida Representative Brian Mast says that Huang indicated he is willing to appear, adding that his resignation as Nvidia CEO "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony.

    "I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar says.

    Huang has said he is committed to supporting America's national security concerns, and the Nvidia board has said it has no reason to believe that either national security or company secrets were compromised, and that it is investigating reports that Huang had a close relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

    Beijing has publicly rejected the spying allegations as a smear.

    However, she was investigated last year as part of a probe into several companies including Megaspeed, over potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of computer servers.

    Authorities said they took her passport in June 2025 to ensure she could not leave Singapore during the investigations.

    Earlier, Megaspeed published a statement saying the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously".

    Dearbail Jordan
    Senior business and economics reporter

    Tucked inside the announcement of Jensen Huang’s departure and his temporary replacement, is the news that Nvidia has appointed its first-ever chair.

    This is a big deal. Part of a company chair’s responsibility is to have oversight of the chief executive. Nvidia has gone without one for more than 30 years.

    Huang often lauded the company’s “flat” management structure. “If you want to empower people, you want to make the organisation as flat as possible so that information travels quickly,” he once said.

    Now, Nvidia’s new boss, whoever that ends up being in the long term, will have someone overseeing them - in this case, Harvey Jones, a tech industry veteran who was the former boss of Synopsys, a chip design software maker.

    Rachel Clun
    Business reporter, in New York

    Jensen Huang’s resignation and the revelations that led up to it have followed a turbulent period for artificial intelligence and tech firms in general, as investors have in recent weeks reacted to the US midterm elections and massive spending on AI infrastructure.

    Stephanie Balaouras, vice president and group research director at market research firm Forrester’s, says Huang’s resignation is "a stress test for the AI boom".

    "If Nvidia stabilises quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience," she says, adding that if Nvidia’s position remains under pressure it would suggest the AI ecosystem is more fragile.

    Eldar Tuvey, is the chief executive of AI procurement platform Vertice. He tells the BBC most of its clients spend money with Nvidia, and one customer has been spending billions.

Huang willing to appear before Congress after resigning from Nvidia over affair allegationspublished at 23:36 GMT 12 NovemberJacob PhillipsLive reporter Image source, ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia over 30 years ago and has has an estimated net worth of $145bn (£109bn)Tech billionaire Jensen Huang has indicated he is willing to appear before Congress to discuss whether US national security was compromised, following a major scandal at one of the most valuable companies in the world.Huang resigned as the CEO of Nvidia, the enormously successful AI chip company, after it was reported he had two affairs: one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and another with senior employee Kimberly Powell.The company's stocks plummeted as US markets opened shortly after Huang's resignation, and while it recovered some ground, it closed more than 4% down, with the firm shedding more than half a trillion in market value.Huang has been replaced for now by the company's Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress who will look to steady the ship at the company.Dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", Huang transformed Nvidia from a video game chip business to develop semiconductors critical for developing AI.Access to advanced computer chips has become a key battleground between Beijing and Washington, writes our China correspondent. A computer chip is essentially a small piece of semiconductor material, or a set of electronic circuits. It processes information and stores data. Nvidia is far from the only company that designs computer chips, which more broadly are used in all modern digital technology, from computers to cars to kitchen appliances. But Nvidia chips are used for many cutting-edge technologies, and are widely used in the AI industry.The company was founded in 1993. Before the AI boom took off, it was largely known for making the type of chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.It has widely been considered a stock market darling in recent years, with the AI boom driving a meteoric rise in its share price.Yesterday - even after allegations that Huang had had affairs caused it to tumble, and with concerns about further AI regulation after the Democrats won Congress - the stock was trading at around $170.
